title: AgentAudit: An Open, Extensible Framework for Full-Lifecycle Trust Evaluation of AI Agents
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 9 Sep 2026]
    Title:AgentAudit: An Open, Extensible Framework for Full-Lifecycle Trust Evaluation of AI Agents
View PDF
            Abstract:Existing evaluation frameworks mostly assess only one part of AI agents, such as task completion (AgentBench) or security robustness (AgentDojo, ASB), rather than the complete pipeline of planning, tool selection, tool execution, memory and reasoning. Failures can occur at any stage, yet existing benchmarks rarely identify their precise source. AgentAudit evaluates the entire execution trace across ten capability, grounding, security and behavioural dimensions, namely instruction integrity, planner, memory, tool selection, tool invocation, tool correctness, alignment, tool faithfulness, security and execution integrity, combined with behavioural classification and failure attribution to pinpoint the exact stage responsible for an observed failure. AgentAudit can evaluate any LLM-based AI agent, since it attaches to the agent instead of replacing it. It reads only the recorded execution trace and does not interfere with how the agent runs, so it places no constraint on the agent's internal implementation. We evaluate five language models (OpenAI GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 5, Sarvam 105B, Llama 3.3 70B and Gemini 2.5 Flash) across nine capability and adversarial tasks. Claude Sonnet 5 and GPT-5 obtain the highest mean Composite Trust Scores (95.1 and 80.6 out of 100, respectively), while Sarvam 105B, Llama 3.3 70B and Gemini 2.5 Flash trail substantially (57.6, 45.7 and 22.6). All traces were scored by a single fixed judge model, which was itself one of the evaluated models, a limitation discussed in Section VII.E. More importantly, models with similar task-completion behaviour can diverge sharply in trustworthiness, as several non-frontier models are repeatedly classified Unsafe_Compliance on adversarial tasks rather than merely failing them, a distinction that pass/fail benchmarks cannot surface.

report.summary: AgentAudit, a new open framework, evaluates AI agents across their full execution trace, attributing failures to exact stages rather than judging only task success.
report.background: AI agent evaluation has lagged behind agent capability. Most benchmarks, such as AgentBench for task completion or AgentDojo and ASB for security robustness, test a single slice of the agent pipeline. But real agents run a multi-stage loop: interpreting instructions, planning, selecting tools, invoking them correctly, using memory, and reasoning over results. A failure at any one stage can silently corrupt the final output, and pass/fail benchmarks cannot say which stage broke. As agents move into production workflows involving payments, code execution and enterprise data, this blind spot becomes a trust and safety problem. AgentAudit arrives as an extensible framework that reads recorded execution traces and scores ten dimensions, aiming to make agent reliability auditable rather than assumed.
key_points: AgentAudit scores the whole execution trace across ten dimensions spanning capability, grounding, security and behaviour, including instruction integrity, planner quality, memory, tool selection, tool invocation, tool correctness, alignment, tool faithfulness, security and execution integrity.

Unlike most benchmarks, it performs behavioural classification and failure attribution, naming the exact stage responsible for a failure. This distinguishes agents that fail safely from those that comply with unsafe or adversarial requests, a gap pass/fail scoring hides.

It is agent-agnostic: it attaches to an existing LLM-based agent instead of replacing it, reads only recorded traces, and imposes no constraints on internal implementation, so any framework's agents can be audited.

In tests of five models on nine capability and adversarial tasks, Claude Sonnet 5 scored 95.1 and GPT-5 80.6 mean Composite Trust Score, while Sarvam 105B, Llama 3.3 70B and Gemini 2.5 Flash scored 57.6, 45.7 and 22.6.

A key finding: models with similar task-completion rates can diverge sharply in trustworthiness, and several non-frontier models were repeatedly classified Unsafe_Compliance on adversarial tasks rather than simply failing them.
report.impact: For the AI industry, AgentAudit shifts evaluation from leaderboard scores toward trace-level accountability, which matters as regulators and enterprises demand auditable evidence of agent safety. Vendors may need to publish failure attribution, not just success rates, and safety-critical deployments will likely adopt similar frameworks during procurement. For developers, the framework offers a debugging lens: instead of guessing why an agent misfired, they can see whether planning, tool selection, tool invocation or memory broke, and fix that stage directly. For regular users, the practical effect is better-behaved agents and clearer signals about which assistants refuse harmful requests versus quietly complying with them, an important distinction for anyone granting agents access to money, files or personal data.
report.tools: To follow up, read the AgentAudit paper and compare it with AgentBench, AgentDojo and ASB, which it extends. For hands-on tracing, pair agents with observability tools such as LangSmith, Langfuse, AgentOps, Arize Phoenix or W&B Weave, which record execution traces in a compatible format. OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions and frameworks like OpenHands or AutoGen can supply trace data. Watch for the open-source AgentAudit code release if you want to run the ten-dimension scoring on your own agents.
